content.intro: This lesson covers What Is Unsafe Rust?. It sits in Module 20, Unsafe Rust and Foreign Function Interfaces, and builds toward a practical Rust mental model rather than memorizing a term in isolation.
content.why_it_matters: What Is Unsafe Rust? matters when you work with unsafe invariants and external contracts. Understanding the rule helps you predict compiler or runtime behavior, document assumptions, and choose a safer implementation when inputs or system conditions change.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Unsafe Rust permits a narrow set of operations whose safety obligations the compiler cannot fully prove. Every unsafe boundary needs explicit invariants, valid initialization, correct aliasing, and compatible external contracts.

content_blocks.title: A reliable way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: For What Is Unsafe Rust?, write down the inputs, the guarantee you expect, and the boundary where that guarantee stops. Work through a minimal example first; then deliberately test one edge case. Treat every unsafe block as a contract with the reader: state the invariants, minimize its scope, and test the safe abstraction built around it.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not assume What Is Unsafe Rust? guarantees more than it actually does. Reduce a failure to a small reproducer, read the full compiler diagnostic or error value, consult the matching official reference, and change one assumption at a time.

content_blocks.title: Toolchain and execution boundary
content_blocks.text: Course examples are static reference snippets, not executed inside CodeLeaf. Most standard-library examples can be tried in a Rust 2024 Cargo project; specialized networking, database, async, procedural-macro, embedded, and WebAssembly scenarios require the toolchain and dependencies described in their lessons.
